stories.body:
Co-published with L.A. Material

Reporting Highlights

Scant Scrutiny: After people died or were hospitalized soon after riding Six Flags’ X2 roller coaster, California regulators often did minimal or no inspection.

Riders’ Responsibility: California regulators have regularly accepted Six Flags’ assertions that riders’ injuries could not be the fault of the X2.

Insufficient Inspectors : A 2025 audit found that the state agency enforcing roller coaster safety had been short-staffed for years.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.

A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.

Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.

Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.

The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.

Christopher’s is a third.

A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.

But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.

“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”

CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.

Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”

Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.

When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”

Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.

The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.

That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.

Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.

It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America.

Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections , and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency.

But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2.

In 16 instances involving people who wound up in the hospital after riding the X2 between 2009 and 2022, CalOSHA invoked identical or similar language after checking a box on accident reports that said state action was not called for. “At this time, this accident does not warrant an investigation,” said one typical form. “The condition which developed while the patron was riding does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride.” The report was filed in response to a woman who was hospitalized in 2016 with a head injury after riding the X2.

This also held true in cases where people lost their lives. When Hilda Farias suffered a massive brain hemorrhage after riding the X2 in October 2010, CalOSHA officials adopted similar language and conducted no inspection. The state regulator’s report did not even note that the 28-year-old mother of a 5-year-old had died, according to records obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material. Farias’ family sued the theme park, and the case settled in 2015.

When Hawley died in June 2022 after riding the X2, Magic Mountain initially told CalOSHA that the cause appeared to be heatstroke, according to a state report. The coroner later determined that Hawley, like Farias, had died of a massive brain hemorrhage. On that occasion, CalOSHA shut the ride down briefly while Six Flags conducted tests to measure the impact of g-forces on the rider and examined maintenance records. It ultimately determined that the ride was operating normally, according to a CalOSHA inspection obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Christopher Gibson wore a Batman hoodie to school almost every day.

Diagnosed with autism when he was 5 or 6, Christopher was “high-functioning and verbal,” his mother told a sheriff’s detective. He had recently graduated high school and was headed to Colorado Mesa University to study theater.

As part of a family tradition, the teen’s mother let each of her five children pick the location of a celebratory senior trip. Chistopher wanted to ride roller coasters, and mother and son discussed a trip to Disneyland or Disney World. After some online research, Christopher chose Six Flags Magic Mountain, known for its thrill rides and DC Comics characters.

“He wanted to see Six Flags,” said Chadwick McGrady, an attorney representing the family in Christopher’s death. “The marketing worked.”

Magic Mountain sits about 35 miles north of downtown Los Angeles, in Valencia, the last notable stop before Interstate 5 climbs a steep stretch known as the Grapevine and drops down into the San Joaquin Valley. The park is aptly named: Roller coasters built into the mountainous terrain hurtle riders down hillsides and through trees, with disorienting turns taken at high velocity.

Christopher rode the X2 on June 2 and again on the morning of June 3. Soon after, reeling from a headache, he texted his mother from a park restroom: “I don’t think I can do any more today. My head is hurting me.”

They went back to the hotel. He had two days to recover before one of the big draws of the trip: DC Heroes and Villains Fest. Christopher “was a huge fan of DC Comics and was looking forward to meeting Batman on Friday, when DC Comics characters would be at the park,” sheriff’s detective Yoon Nam would later write in her report. Friday, June 5, was its opening day, and Christopher was determined not to miss it.

But on the morning of June 4, his head was still hurting him. He had taken refuge in the hotel room’s closet. His mother wasn’t unduly alarmed, because Christopher often retreated to dark spaces at home, a longstanding self-soothing ritual. She listened to the sound of his snoring — until at some point in the afternoon, the sound stopped.

In a statement released through her lawyer, Fascaldo said that her son “had so many dreams, and had his whole life ahead of him.”

After an autopsy, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner found a large subdural hemorrhage. The cause of death: “blunt force head trauma.” The reason for the injuries was noted as a “history of theme park rides.”

Nam and the medical examiner spoke by phone with Fascaldo, Christopher’s mother, on June 6.

According to a source familiar with the investigation, Fascaldo was composed, recounting a precise chronology of the rides Christopher had ridden. Among them were Full Throttle and the Viper, and, at least twice, the X2.

Nam contacted CalOSHA. She knew that it was responsible for regulating the state’s roller coasters and wanted to make sure the agency was aware that the Magic Mountain rides could have contributed to Christopher’s death.

“I cannot attribute his death to his roller coaster ride experiences with 100% certainty,” Nam wrote in a July 2 email to Bobby Park, who runs the CalOSHA unit regulating roller coasters. “However, at this time, it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.”

The detective offered to help. “Please let me know if this case warrants additional follow-up by your office,” she wrote. “Feel free to call, text, or email with any questions or concerns.”

In the days after that unanswered email, more parkgoers suffered injuries after riding the X2.

On the evening of July 5, three days after the homicide detective sent her email, Pamela Guillen, 39, rode the coaster with her daughter.

When the car she was riding in trundled back into the station, Guillen’s daughter saw that her mother was “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” according to a lawsuit the family recently filed. Six Flags has not yet filed a response.

Guillen, who was visiting from Hawaii, managed to stumble off the ride, but a few minutes later park EMTs found her lying unconscious at the exit ramp. Two hours later, Gary Newman, the park’s vice president of maintenance, phoned CalOSHA to report the accident, relaying that a relative had said: “My cousin seemed out of it when she got off the ride so we took her to a bench and she went unconscious.”

The next morning, Scott Prather, a senior safety engineer with CalOSHA’s theme park unit, emailed his boss. According to a state official who has viewed the email, Guillen had been diagnosed with a brain bleed and was going into surgery. The email also said that the ride had been closed for inspection and g-force testing to ensure it was operating as intended.

Six Flags hired a firm that specialized in amusement park rides to conduct the test, according to a CalOSHA source familiar with the investigation.

State officials reviewed the results and authorized Magic Mountain to reopen the ride, the source said.

Then, on July 9, there was another incident, according to CalOSHA records reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. A woman from Nevada was visiting Magic Mountain with her family and others. They were roller coaster enthusiasts and had saved the X2 for their last ride of the day.

As soon as the ride started, the woman sensed something was wrong, according to an email she later sent to CalOSHA’s general inbox.

“The back of my head was repeatedly and forcefully slammed against the back of the seat,” she wrote in the email, which was reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. “I tried holding my head forward and tried pushing it back against the seat to stop the banging, neither worked.”

When the ride stopped, she wasn’t sure whether she could stand. She couldn’t turn her head from side to side. She had nausea, sensitivity to light and a headache that reached “approximately 9 out of 10.”

She wasn’t the only one. “Three of the eight people riding together experienced similar difficulty with their heads repeatedly striking the backs of their seats,” she wrote in August.

She also filed a formal complaint with Six Flags in July but has not received a response, she told ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Two days after the Nevada woman rode the X2, there was another, more serious injury.

Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, a healthy 25-year-old from Los Angeles, rode the X2 on the night of July 11.

According to a lawsuit her family filed in September against the park, Greer-Wilkinson came off the ride “confused and having difficulty walking.” She stumbled off and then lost consciousness. She has since had multiple emergency brain surgeries. The lawsuit says she “remains bedridden, ventilator dependent, unable to speak.” Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuit.

On July 12, the X2 was temporarily shut down. It has not reopened.

In the wake of the ride’s closure, many amusement park patrons are asking how regulators could have missed so many signs of danger.

California law requires CalOSHA to audit records related to every permanent ride each year, including reports of accidents. When amusement park patrons are seriously injured on rides, the theme park must notify regulators immediately .

And yet, again and again, records show, regulators accepted Six Flags’ assertions that the injuries people suffered were not the fault of the X2. ProPublica and L.A. Material reviewed the state’s reports on X2 riders who were taken to the hospital from 2009 to 2022. In more than two-thirds of the cases, or 17 out 23, CalOSHA checked “no” on the form that would determine whether an investigation was warranted.

In September 2022, less than three months after Hawley died, a 28-year-old woman passed out as she exited the ride and hit her head, according to Magic Mountain’s account of the accident in a report filed with the state Paramedics took her to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.

Two days after the woman’s injury, Park determined no investigation was necessary. Park wrote: “Patron has pre-existing TBI [traumatic brain injury], diabetes, and has not eaten or consumed anything throughout the day.”

The woman, who survived the incident, sued Six Flags, which denied fault. The case settled in 2025.

The pattern of regulators citing preexisting conditions or rider behavior went back years. In 2011, the state noted that a 21-year-old woman had “a history of panic attacks,” so no investigation of the ride was necessary after she complained of a head injury.

In 2016, a 49-year-old woman hit her head against the headrest and asked for an ambulance. CalOSHA noted that her condition “does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride,” adding that she “did not keep her head back” as riders are instructed.

Park declined to comment.

Some of the failures appear related to staffing shortages at CalOSHA. According to a 2025 staffing study by a Sacramento consulting firm commissioned by the state, audits of amusement park rides can be brief. The annual audit for a ride in X2’s class — a review meant to cover accident reports, training and maintenance reports and inspections — lasted an average of 3.7 hours.

The study also found that CalOSHA’s ride unit had been short-staffed for at least three years, with vacancies for its top job and two of four supervisor posts. There were “insufficient” supervisors for “thorough field supervision” and “inspection report review,” the report found.

Documents obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material show Park had voiced frustration about staffing for his division since at least 2019. In an email he sent last week to his supervisor and the state department that oversees CalOSHA, Park wrote: “We have done workload studies, classification studies, begged, pleaded, and warned of the impending doom, and we are still no further along than we were 11 years ago.”

He continued: “We have failed. I have tried to do this, but I cannot continue as the dwindling supply of tools has run out.”

Park had been the CalOSHA official who received the news of Christopher Gibson’s death from Nam, the homicide detective, in early July.

In late August, after the X2 had been closed for more than a month, the detective sent a follow-up email to Park about the teen’s death.

“I never heard back from you regarding my previous email,” Nam wrote. “I saw news about multiple injuries involving the X2 ride at the Six Flags. Is there anything else I need to do?”

Park finally wrote back: “Apologies, I thought we responded.”

Park told the detective that since Christopher had died in a hotel room, there was no way to confirm which roller coasters the teen had ridden and “it would be difficult to determine which ride to assign this to or if it even is associated with a ride.”

Still, a few weeks later, state officials ordered a more sophisticated g-force test of the ride, citing a series of injuries and a death over the summer. CalOSHA said in a statement that there are limits to commonly used ride testing. The standard test focuses on the torso and does not “necessarily establish the full range of movement or physical impacts experienced by an individual rider, including the potential effects on the head and neck,” the agency said. The order for new g-force testing didn’t mention anyone by name, but it did refer to an incident on June 3, the day Christopher left the park with a headache and eventually retreated to his hotel room’s closet, where he died.

The test results are pending.

Later in September, Six Flags announced the ride’s permanent shuttering without acknowledging the injuries or deaths connected with the roller coaster. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding said in a statement . “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”

stories.title: Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters
stories.summary: Venezuelans deserve democracy before, not after, a military deal with the United States. The post Venezuela’s Base Deal Has No Voters appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .

stories.body:
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez during a press conference regarding the oil agreement reached by the US government and Venezuela on September 2, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela. (Jesus Vargas/Getty Images)

In his first week as Venezuela’s foreign minister, Oliver Blanco sat down with Marco Rubio at the State Department on November 2. The official readout spoke of electoral reforms, political prisoners and the president’s three-phase plan : stabilization first, then economic recovery and reconciliation, and only then a democratic transition. It said nothing about soldiers.

A day later, The New York Times reported that the State Department, under Rubio, is negotiating a status of forces agreement with Caracas that would lay the foundation for a long-term American military presence. Troop numbers and locations would be settled in later agreements.

Washington will sell this as paperwork. The State Department says it has negotiated such pacts with more than 100 countries, which give American forces a predictable legal footing for ship visits, training, and exercises. Seen from outside Washington, Venezuela is not merely the latest entry on that list. It is a country whose president was seized by American troops on January 3 , whose interim leader holds no electoral mandate, and whose oil now carries a Pentagon stake.

A status of forces agreement signed under those conditions does not regulate a relationship between two sovereign governments. It writes a protectorate into law before the protected get a vote.

The soldiers, in fact, are arriving ahead of the lawyers. On October 30, Venezuelan drones and helicopters struck a Colombian National Liberation Army (ELN) camp in Apure state near the border with Colombia, and four U.S. officials told The Times that Washington supplied intelligence and drone support. The border rights group FundaRedes counted 23 victim s . Back in June, a Southern Command airstrike killed Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flores, a founder of Tren de Aragua, with CIA intelligence and Venezuelan forces taking part. After the June earthquakes, about 2,000 American troops moved into and around the country before pulling out again. The reopened U.S. embassy in Caracas already has a military attaché.

The readout leaves out an important motive for a future military base: the oil fields. In September, the administration announced a deal giving Washington a stake in about one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil resources. Caracas handed North American Blue Energy Partners, the vehicle of oilman Alejandro Betancourt, 100-year rights over 17 oilfields holding 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The Pentagon owns 35 percent of that company, and Washington is guaranteed the right to buy a fifth of its output at cost.

Nobody leaves a century-long concession, part-owned by the Defense Department, without a guard. Donald Trump , speaking in Washington the same Monday Blanco visited, did not bother with euphemism. He referred to “our conquest of Venezuela.” Oil contracts are written for decades. So, it seems, are the garrisons that guard them.

Latin America has lived through this imbroglio before. In 1901, Cuba had to accept the Platt Amendment before American forces would leave, and the State Department’s historians list among its conditions the sale or lease of land for naval stations. The Guantánamo lease followed in February 1903. Washington repealed the amendment in 1934 and kept the lease, and the naval base still operates. The political tutelage was renegotiated. The military footprint signed during the tutelage outlived everyone who signed it.

The interim authority across the table from Rubio is in no position to bargain hard, and it has no mandate to bargain at all. Delcy Rodríguez has given no election date. Trump says Venezuela is not ready for elections. María Corina Machado, back after ten months in exile, wants a presidential vote by July. On Monday, teachers, nurses and university unions held a 12-hour national stoppage , demanding a $960 year-end payment that the government had left unanswered . The minimum monthly income stands at $240 . A government that cannot settle with its teachers is settling the legal status of foreign soldiers. Venezuelans can read that order of priorities. So can every capital in the hemisphere.

The counterargument deserves a fair hearing. Status of forces agreements are mundane instruments, and most of them govern exercises rather than occupations. The ELN and Tren de Aragua are real, and a Venezuelan army that sheltered guerrillas for years is now bombing them. The State Department insists that no base talks are under way.

But that is exactly the design of the deal. The framework comes first, and everything that matters (numbers, locations, duration) would be part of follow-on arrangements that neither an elected Venezuelan legislature nor the U.S. Senate will ever vote on.

The Democratic majorities that won both chambers on November 3 have three ways to keep this interim arrangement from hardening.

First, demand the text. State Department officials briefed some congressional aides on the talks in late October. A briefing for aides is not oversight.

Second, insist on the treaty form. Basing and status arrangements are usually concluded as executive agreements, not treaties. Venezuela is the case for the exception. An open-ended military presence in a country the United States attacked 10 months ago is the kind of commitment the Constitution leaves to two-thirds of the Senate.

Third, use the purse. A rider barring funds for any permanent presence in Venezuela until an elected government ratifies the arrangement would cost Washington nothing it needs this year. It would cost the oil concession its armed guarantee, and for obvious reasons the White House will fight it.

The timing gives the game away. If Rubio signs the agreement before the new Congress convenes in January, an outgoing majority and an unelected partner will have settled the matter between them, and Venezuelans will inherit the deal the way Cubans inherited Guantánamo. If the deal waits for a Senate vote and an elected government in Caracas, it may still go through. At least it will have voters behind it.

stories.title: The Incredible Shrinking Superpower
stories.summary: The failing war with Iran marks a dramatic retreat by the U.S. from the Middle East. The post The Incredible Shrinking Superpower appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
An attendee dressed like Uncle Sam waits for Republican presidential nominee, former U.S. President Donald Trump to arrive for a campaign rally at the Mosack Group warehouse on September 25, 2024 (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Originally published in Tom Dispatch .

The failure of Tel Aviv and Washington to achieve their war aims in Iran has resulted in the most dramatic American retreat from a region since the U.S. flight from Vietnam in 1975. This startling American defeat — after a generation of forever war failures and stalemates — has been thrown into broad relief by the resumption of another regional conflict that has received far less attention than the Trump administration’s sputtering war with Tehran. This fall, the forces that most Americans know as “the Houthis” have conducted a blitzkrieg in their native Yemen and have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure with missiles and drones. In doing so, they have put a spotlight on the limits of American power, and the shrinking U.S. military footprint, in the Middle East.

The long-standing conflict between Saudi Arabia and northern Yemen’s Ansarullah, or “Helpers of God,” led by the Houthi clan, heated up again in July 2026, when Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing on its return from the funeral in Iran for slain Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The Ansarullah government launched its own attacks and, in October, managed briefly to close Saudi Arabia’s own airport. The renewed war has now expanded into a regional conflict, with Pakistan, Türkiye, and, recently, Egypt pledging to defend the kingdom from attack, though none of these regional powers appear eager to conduct operations in Yemen itself. Notably absent from the current conflict is Saudi Arabia’s most powerful ally, the United States, since President Donald Trump has repeatedly declined to intervene on behalf of his Saudi allies.

The typical U.S. press framing of Ansarullah as an “Iran-backed militia” is inaccurate, since the movement has local, Arab nationalist reasons for its actions and is a full-scale government that rules some 80 percent of Yemen’s population. Still, it does receive surreptitious technical and military support from Iran, though nothing like the hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech armaments — from kits turning 2,000-pound “dumb” bombs into precision munitions to advanced air-to-air missiles — that the U.S. provides the Saudis. Ironically, Trump’s war on Iran, fought in conjunction with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, weakened the Saudis and exposed their vulnerabilities to military attack by Iranian drones and missiles, impelling them to seek a symbolic win over a less formidable enemy in neighboring Yemen. But the weaknesses exposed by Iran’s drones helped encourage a vigorous Ansarullah rejoinder.

The Incredible Shrinking Superpower

The American refusal to join Saudi Arabia’s war signals a profound degradation in U.S. capabilities and standing in the Middle East. The U.S. military had, for decades, dominated the region from a network of about 20 major bases. The U.S. Navy operated out of the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet in Manama, Bahrain. The U.S. Air Force flew missions from the massive al-Udeid Air Base in Qatar, which housed 10,000 U.S. personnel. Thousands of ground troops were barracked in Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan. The Pentagon admitted that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict. In addition, dozens of U.S. aircraft were destroyed or damaged during OEF.”

The naval base at Manama, one of America’s most important naval facilities and headquarters of the Navy’s Fifth Fleet, was destroyed by Iranian strikes. (Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao admitted last month that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”) The loss of Manama led to supply shortages and poor morale aboard the USS Lincoln and other ships patrolling the Strait of Hormuz, bedeviling Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

The CIA offices at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh were annihilated . Iran struck al-Udeid’s evacuated Combined Air Operations Center in Qatar, from which the Pentagon had directed its strikes on enemies as diverse as the Taliban and ISIL over recent decades, and rendered this facility inoperable . All U.S. troops were also withdrawn from Iraq, a process accelerated by the inability of U.S. missile interceptors to protect them from attacks by Iran and allied Shiite militias there.

Iran’s deployment of swarms of Shahed drones caused the United States and Israel to use up much of their stock of interceptors , which are time-consuming and expensive to replace. A basic Shahed costs as little as $20,000, though new hardened versions are more expensive — whereas a Patriot interceptor costs $4 million. One reason the Trump administration may be reluctant to intervene in Yemen is that if the U.S. cannot fly missions from al-Udeid, and cannot be sure any new fighter-jet fleets stationed in the region will be safe from Iran, given the paucity of interceptors, the Pentagon will have a limited ability to rescue any U.S. pilots shot down over Yemen.

America’s Profound Weakness in the Middle East

Saudi Arabia launched a war against the ascendant Ansarullah in 2015 when the latter staged a coup in the capital of Sanaa. The Ansarullah movement is rooted in Yemen’s Zaidi Shiism, though it is more radical than traditional Zaidism. (Zaidi Shiism differs substantially from Iranian Shiism, having no ayatollahs and having relatively good relations with Sunnis.)

About a third of Yemenis are Zaidis, who predominate in the north of the country, and many have long resented the dominance of their politics and culture by neighboring, oil-rich, Sunni Saudi Arabia, whose official ideology is hard-line Wahhabism, a puritanical form of Islam that insists on a literal interpretation of the Quran. Wahhabi proselytizing among the Shia enraged the Houthi clan and their followers began rebelling against the government of military dictator Ali Abdullah Saleh in 2004. But when he was deposed by popular demonstrations during the Arab Spring in 2012, Saleh gradually allied with the Houthis, and by 2015 about half the Yemeni military rallied to their side, along with some major Sunni tribes.

In response to the Houthis’ rise, a Saudi-led coalition that included the United Arab Emirates began bombing Yemen in 2015. Until 2022, the U.S, then militarily dominant in the region, provided the Saudis with strategic advice, weaponry, and in-air refueling for their fighter jets in the Yemen war, though Riyadh’s tendency to bomb civilian infrastructure rather than confining themselves to military targets caused tension between the two allies. While the Saudis and their coalition pushed the Houthis out of much of the south of the country, including Aden, they were unable to dislodge them from the north. The Saudis implicitly acknowledged their failure with a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022 , which largely held until this past summer.

The Forever Wars Effect

America’s forever wars against Middle Eastern countries that decline to accept the Israel project or American corporate neocolonialism helped reignite the Saudi–Yemeni conflict. Iran is the last major state in the region that rejects Israel and is off-limits to U.S. corporate investment, a stance that inspires much of Washington’s animus. Netanyahu was therefore easily able to persuade Trump, as a privileged visitor to the White House Situation Room, to attack Iran in February.

The glib expectation of Netanyahu and of his Mossad chief at that time, David Barnea, that the Islamic Republic would crumble if Israel murdered Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and around 50 other high-ranking regime figures proved wishful thinking . The notion that Iran was vulnerable to a tightened petroleum blockade was turned on its head by the hard-liners who ascended to power after Khamenei’s death. Largely veterans of the grueling eight-year Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s, the country’s new leaders pursued a policy of “de-basing” toward the United States, taking out its main regional military facilities.

In addition, Iran launched precision strikes at the energy facilities of their Arab Gulf neighbors who had hosted those American bases. They struck Kuwait’s national petroleum company and its fields and refineries. They took out 17 percent of the production of Qatar’s Ras Laffan natural gas facility, even though Doha had good relations with Tehran and had mediated for Iran. Tehran also struck ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using missiles and drones, scaring the major shipping insurers into withdrawing their contracts. Few shipping magnates would risk cargoes worth billions of dollars without insurance.

Iran threw the world into an energy crisis reminiscent of the 1970s, which would have been even more devastating had China not released oil from its vast private and public petroleum reserves and cut its oil imports from 11.5 million barrels a day to under 9 million barrels a day, a move partially enabled by its turn to electric vehicles, which saved it 1.5 million barrels a day. High gasoline and diesel prices hurt Asia more than the United States, but prices rose globally. A third of the world’s helium, essential for cooling computer chips in the production process, comes from the Gulf, and that supply was also interrupted, increasing the price of electronics.

By successfully striking Saudi Arabia, Iran demonstrated that the kingdom’s ability to protect itself is imperfect and its infrastructure is vulnerable. By blockading the Strait of Hormuz in a way that the United States had difficulty undoing, Iran demonstrated the vulnerability of key world maritime arteries, something Ansarullah had already highlighted by striking at shipping in the Red Sea to protest the Gaza genocide.

Blockade for Blockade

When the Saudis bombed Sanaa’s airport in July 2026, Ansarullah’s leadership appears to have decided that Riyadh posed an ongoing existential danger to their state and sought to strangle the Yemeni economy, just as Israel had done to Gaza . Moreover, they sensed that the kingdom could be rolled back in the wake of the failure of the Israeli–U.S. war on Iran. Just as Iran had weakened the Gulf Arab states with its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis believed they could seriously degrade the Saudi economy by blocking Riyadh’s shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, “the Strait of Tears,” between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

Saudi exports through the Strait of Hormuz had fallen substantially. The kingdom did, however, have an escape valve: its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Ships loading at Yanbu then headed for Saudi Arabia’s major Asian markets through the Bab al-Mandab. If Ansarullah could make the tanker captains fearful of this transit, they could reduce Saudi Arabia’s income even further. The Houthi spokesperson, Muhammad Abd al-Salam, warned that the prohibition of Saudi shipping was only the first step in a tit-for-tat strategy of “blockade for blockade.” The idea wasn’t original. The Saudis and the U.S. had often attempted to blockade petroleum imports to northern Yemen during the seven-year Saudi–Yemeni War.

In the subsequent three months, Ansarullah deployed missiles and drones constructed from Iranian models by military engineers trained by the old nationalist government of Ali Abdullah Saleh, many of whom had joined the Ansarullah military, in what has been called a Yemeni “ military industrial complex .”

Just as the kingdom’s interceptors had proven unable to prevent Iranian strikes on targets such as the CIA section of the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, they sometimes failed to halt the barrage of Yemeni missiles and drones. Refineries and oil installations, even the headquarters of the state oil giant, Saudi Aramco, in Dhahran, were hit. In October, Ansarullah closed Riyadh’s International Airport, just as the Saudis had attempted to close that of Sanaa in July. Ansarullah also surged out of their mountain strongholds and made a major push to Yemen’s southwest coast, taking the strategic port of Mocha overlooking the Bab al-Mandab. They also moved on Taiz , an inland industrial city of nearly 1 million inhabitants, one of the last major population centers not already under their control, in a campaign that tested the ability of the small Saudi-backed government of Rashad al-Alimi in Aden to resist it.

Highlanders and Oil Sheikhs

Just as the Vietnam War was one conflict among many fought in the Third World during the Cold War between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, so the Saudi–Yemeni War of 2026 is part of the larger struggle between the U.S. and Israel and Iran. Still, just as Vietnam was more about Vietnamese anticolonialism, nationalism, and sovereignty than about Communism and the ownership of the means of production, so the Saudi–Yemeni War is about Yemeni autonomy more than it is about the loose Houthi alliance with Iran. The conflict is not primarily between Zaidism and Wahhabism, though religious tensions are part of the story, but is far more rooted in a struggle between desperately poor Yemeni highlanders and fabulously wealthy Saudi sheikhs.

The plutocratic Saudi ruling elite is closely tied to Washington and has secret dealings with the Israelis, with whom it shares a distrust of the poverty-stricken Palestinian resistance, and views Ansarullah as cat’s paws of Iran in the Arabian Peninsula and as radical republicans trying to overthrow the region’s oil monarchies in favor of populism. For its part, Ansarullah are Arab nationalists, anti-American, and seek to use oil resources for populist purposes. And they have been willing to attack Israel to defend the Palestinians of Gaza from genocide.

Last week, Ansarullah battered targets across Saudi Arabia, prompting a further pullback from the region by Washington. The Yemeni forces attacked King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. An Ansarullah spokesperson said the group also targeted the Saudi defense ministry in the capital, Riyadh, along with an Aramco site in Yanbu, and an airport in the southern city of Abha. Reports also emerged of an attack on another Aramco oil field.

“Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure,” wrote State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott in an October 21 post on X, after the wave of attacks, ordering “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” out of Saudi Arabia.

It’s just the latest evidence of the most significant regional retreat by the U.S. in half a century and evidence of profound American military decline. The outcome of their war with the Saudis will not determine the issue of the U.S.–Israeli contest with Iran, but the very ability of Ansarullah to prosecute it points to the profound weakening of the American posture in the Middle East.

stories.body:
We are witnessing one of the biggest generational conflicts in decades: a global revolution against a gerontocracy.

John Last is a freelance journalist and former foreign correspondent living outside Ottawa, Canada.

Across Europe, young people are being arrested in their thousands. In Milan, jackbooted soldiers from the Italian military — average age, 38 — haul protesters, some of whom are as young as 12 and 13, away from picket lines and into armored vehicles. Italy’s government — average age, 60 — has passed a new decree allowing detainments for up to 24 hours without charge. Vandals can now be arrested 48 hours after their crimes; Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, 53, has called for their parents to face financial penalties too.

Italy’s weekend of protests at the end of October, in at least a dozen major cities, was the most destructive in recent memory. In Milan, hooded youths looted the city’s luxury stores, pilfering products, one reporter wrote , “that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.” But as shocking as Italy’s protests have been, they pale in comparison to those in France. Mobs of people have paralyzed city centers across the country for weeks. The grand streets of Paris have been blanketed in acrid smoke. French President Emmanuel Macron has accused an alliance of “radical far-left groups [and] criminals” of trying “to bring down the Republic.” Fifty-three police officers were injured over the course of a single weekend.

After more than a month, it is almost hard to believe that protests of this magnitude began over the failures of a university application portal . But by now, the grievances have multiplied: the high cost of fuel, the crowding of schools, the inaccessibility of housing, the growing precarity of work. In turn, the protests have taken on an existential desperation. An unmistakable vibe of despair permeates the masked protesters. “They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can’t say anything,” one protester in Paris told the BBC. “It’s been too long, it’s been too much.”

“They” are the elder-elite of Europe, the now-aged baby boomers who greedily gobbled up the assets of their societies: a third of Italy’s housing stock; a quarter of France’s public spending; 98% of the average Spanish worker’s salary, in the form of monthly rent. While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — they cash in. Rising prices, precarious work, broken schools: As a generation, the boomers have remained largely unaffected while the value of their real estate and investments boomed. As their wealth and number grew, they came to set the agendas of unions, politicians and the media, and they bent the state to suppress any who would rally against them. They pioneered a playbook to extract the last cents of value from Europe’s bloated and aging welfare states before departing a world they leave on the threshold of self-destruction.

But the underclass in their wake cannot be restrained forever. In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long; like the dwarves of Moria, they accidentally unleashed a primal foe. “It has been called the children’s war,” La Repubblica reports : an insurgency against calcifying Western gerontocracies waged by their own offspring.

“While young people reel from crisis to crisis — wars, economic stagnation, climate disaster, a pandemic — the now-aged baby boomers cash in.”

In some ways, generational inequality is felt before it can be measured. It is usually assumed that people naturally accumulate wealth over their lifetime, and that a person in their ‘70s should own more in assets than a relatively new worker in their ‘30s. But it wasn’t always so. Today’s old-age security is the result of a general crisis of elder poverty that proliferated across the Western world in the 1920s and ‘30s when people still literally worked themselves to death, or else died penniless. To solve this problem, states embraced a system of “asymmetric socialization,” according to Pieter Vanhuysse, a leading expert in political demography at the University of Southern Denmark. In short, the state took care of the elderly while the family was still mostly expected to take care of the young.

Today, it is hard to imagine a crisis of elder poverty on a similar scale to that of the 1930s, not least because the elderly account for such a large percentage of the population. In France and Italy, thanks to longer lifespans and low rates of reproduction, the number of citizens over 65 has doubled since the arrival of the boomer generation, born between 1946 and 1964, to one in five and one in four residents, respectively. Nor is the phenomenon limited to Europe. In the United States, where fertility rates are higher, the median age has risen by 10 years since 1960. There are fewer than a billion seniors in the world today; by 2060, that number is expected to double and account for a fifth of global population.

As seniors have exploded in number, they have exercised an ever-greater influence on politics. In France, the United Kingdom, Germany, the U.S. and many other developed nations, those aged 65 and over are between 10% and 20% more likely to vote than those aged 18-25. This has contributed to a shocking representative gap — people under 30 account for half of the world’s population but just 2% of its legislators. “There’s a clear representational deficit,” said Daniel Stockemer, a political scientist at the University of Ottawa. “It creates a problem that youth’s concerns are not taken sufficiently into consideration, that youth are not sufficiently included in decision-making processes.”

In a study of intergenerational fairness in state spending, Vanhuysse found a disproportionate favoritism toward the old in nearly all the countries surveyed. Nearly a quarter of young Europeans and nearly half of young Americans are struggling financially; they will also disproportionately bear the weight of the ecological destruction and public debt accumulated by the boomers.

France, where youth first took to the streets, is among the worst offenders. There, public debt now exceeds the value of its economy. In Vanhuysse’s index, it ranks just behind Japan for the disproportionate political power it grants the elderly — nearly two in five civil servants are over 50 , a number that has rapidly increased since 2011. Vanhuysse estimates roughly $5 is spent on elderly citizens for every $1 spent on youth. That is clearly evident in the crumbling, overcrowded schools and inadequate universities that first spurred young people onto the streets. State pensions, meanwhile, eat up a quarter of the country’s public spending — including a whole third of the education ministry’s budget.

“Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic.”

All of this would not be so galling if it were not for the fact that the generation now draining state coffers already benefited from an unprecedented golden age of growth. Boomers entered the workforce at the peak of unionization and enjoyed stable employment, wages that beat inflation and guaranteed pensions upon retirement. They were buying starter homes when housing could be had for just two or three years’ income. Today it is nearly 10 .

Boomers used this unprecedented growth to acquire assets well beyond their needs, sitting on valuable housing stock — 28% of family homes in the U.S., for example — desperately desired by the next generation. Then they leveraged those assets to squeeze younger generations. In Australia, seniors’ investment in rental properties has increased 1,500% at the same time as rents have nearly doubled. Where boomers were able to buy property cheaply and grow their money in investments, young people today spend a vast percentage of their earnings on rent — which, more often than not, is passive income for elderly landlords.

The result is a generation that feels it has been actively held back from achieving the same or better lives than their parents had by that same generation’s relentless extraction of money. Today, Vanhuysse found, a working person in France can expect their lifetime wealth to be 17% lower than that of a baby boomer. “That’s the same difference as being, today in France, a parent of two or a parent of none,” Vanhuysse said, or “of being — hold on for this — a migrant in France or not a migrant in France.”

Far from demonstrating concern for their children, boomers have become the archetype of the hectoring elder, demanding young people live in grim austerity or else be accused of moral failing. Meanwhile, they have led the charge against any policies that would address this imbalance: cuts to pension funding, extensions of the retirement age, freezes on rent, ends to tax breaks on capital gains, the construction of new housing. They have insisted on their right to rent-seek, to economically stunt their own children’s generation. And worse, they have, where possible, actively enshrined this inequality in law.

In the last 10 years, we’ve witnessed the emergence of a two-tiered economy: one offering secure employment and benefits to senior workers and a select few entrants, and a precarious gig economy for anyone else. Nowhere is this clearer than in Italy, which deflated a staggering 42% youth unemployment rate by passing a law allowing for short-term contracts — but only for workers hired after 2014. Today, 40% of those under 29 struggle with precarious employment, compared to just 5% of those over 50. Read Noema in print.

“In the spasms across Europe, we are witnessing a generational uprising, a war on the reckless landlordism of the last propertied generation. They gouged too deep and for too long.”

Italy’s example is particularly stark, but this phenomenon plays out, with slight variations, across the Western world. As a union steward for Canada’s public broadcaster, I witnessed it firsthand: entrenched, often incompetent or disengaged elderly employees guaranteed healthy pensions and generous leave, enabled by the labor of an army of precarious young temps who were denied benefits, moved around and kept on exploitative short-term contracts, always hoping for some vanishing chance at security. The union fought tooth and nail to protect its incumbents; new workers, meanwhile, were expected to “do the time” in employment conditions that their elders had never been asked to endure.

The advent of AI and the ongoing liberalization of the marketplace have only added fuel to this dumpster fire, eliminating entry-level positions, complicating hiring with meaningless and time-consuming tests, and generally increasing the demands of employers. Those under 40 have probably lost count of the major economic disruptions they have been expected to adapt to (I can still remember when we were all being told to learn to code ). Now, still working their way toward stable jobs, home ownership and families, they are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their jobs, it may well collapse the economy instead.

Amid all this chaos, young people have been largely left to fend for themselves. It’s no coincidence that the underfunding of schools prompted this outbreak of violence: Despite a staggering rise in the diagnosis of learning disabilities, classes are often crammed with more students per teacher than ever before. Ten percent of teaching hours go untaught in France because of chronic teacher absenteeism. Parents, too, have taken leave of their responsibilities. One of the possible defenses of Vanhuysse’s “asymmetric socialization” is that, while seniors benefit from wealth transfers via taxes, parents transfer wealth to their children in the form of time — the equivalent of up to seven months’ wages a year, Vanhuysse estimated . But can we really say that’s the case when Gen Z and Gen Alpha are partly defined by the countless hours they were left glued to a screen, largely unsupervised, the unfiltered internet doing untold damage to their psyches?

Elders and politicians love to blame social media for a worrying rise in youth extremism and violence. But that’s not the only cause of the dark, seething nihilism at the heart of the generations now coming of age. Stockemer calls it a “vicious cycle of political alienation”: politicians serve elderly interests, young people disengage from politics and the next government has even less motivation to address their concerns. It has reached the point that politicians openly talk about younger generations as though they are an enemy and treat them accordingly by suspending many of their rights. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has pioneered new methods in the overpolicing of the young: banning raves, lowering the age of criminal culpability and increasing juvenile detention by 50%. A communique from the October 17 Movement, one of the organizing groups behind Italy’s protests, captures the new reality: “A government that responds to the dissatisfaction of a generation with soldiers, handcuffs and decrees does not want to listen.”

But if governments won’t listen, why won’t the boomers who elect them? How can the outpouring of despair on the streets of Europe’s capitals not be enough to move them to cede some of their wealth to the next in line?

If it feels like theirs is a generation for whom no amount of money is enough, it may be because many of them genuinely feel that way, and for good reason. A lot of them grew up believing a millionaire was a rarefied thing. But now, a million dollars is barely enough to guarantee that a 65-year-old will spend their final years in comfort. The so-called “peak boomers” turning 65 between now and 2030 can reasonably expect to live another 20 years, and medical advancements may continue to extend their lifetimes. If they stop earning and investing, they will become victims of the same economic forces they unleashed on younger generations. High housing costs are preventing many seniors from downsizing as expected, high inflation is eating into the value of benefits and the side hustles and part-time jobs that once saved seniors from penury are scarcer than ever.

Looming behind this fear is the privatized eldercare market, which has become the norm in Europe as it has long been in North America. In European countries, the average home care starts at more than $1,000 per month and only climbs from there. Residential care can cost seniors or their families tens of thousands every year. The savings that were supposed to fund the “great wealth transfer” — the mass inheritance of more than $100 trillion in assets accumulated by boomers over their lifetime — are instead being siphoned away by an oligarchy of health care companies. No wonder medically assisted suicide is becoming more popular.

The reality is that neoliberal capitalism of the kind long championed by Macron has proven to be not very good at taking care of anyone except those now at liberty to make a lot more capital. The renowned French economist Thomas Piketty pointed out that the unprecedented 20% cut in per-student funding that prompted France’s protests came at a time when, according to some measures, “France has never been richer.” At the same time as public debt has ballooned out of control, the country’s privately held wealth has doubled in proportion to the country’s GDP, “with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes.” “The problem to solve,” he wrote, “is simply one of distribution.”

In this way, these protests are revealing all sorts of new solidarities — not only between youth struggling to pay rent and seniors fearful of the cost of care, but between the disillusioned elite of European universities and the underpaid truck drivers of Italy, or the migrant teenager from the banlieues and the middle-class couples who can’t afford a child. All are part of the growing class of losers in the economy of today — an economy fatally consumed by presentism, unable and unwilling to consider the greater, long-term good.

Gerontocracy is certainly a contributor to that problem — after all, old people have less of a stake in the future. But in reality, the petty landlord milking tenants, the civil servant counting his days to retirement and the teenager looting Decathlon have much in common: They are all dogs fighting for scraps.

“Still working their way toward stable jobs, affording homes and having families, young people are bracing for a reality where, if AI doesn’t steal their job, it may well collapse the economy instead.”

This is perhaps the thing that earlier protesters in the historic youth uprisings in Nepal and India were able to see much more clearly than their counterparts in the more affluent regions of Europe, and may indeed be behind their relative success. Hopelessness is infectious, and we’re in a pandemic. There is little to separate a trucker who cannot pay for their gas from a student who cannot pay for their rent. Both are facing a profound existential crisis for which they bear little, if any, responsibility — a crisis their governments feel duty-bound to ignore.

It is in moments like this that the extraparliamentary politics of the street flourish. In some sense, this is a return to form for the politics of Europe. “We are quite used to the idea that everything should be oriented towards consensus,” Enrico Biale, an associate professor of political philosophy at University of Piemonte Orientale, told me. “Any form of strong protest is considered a challenge that needs to be contained aggressively.” But 50 years ago, discontented students flooded the ranks of the Red Army Faction and the Brigate Rosse , which terrorized fascist sympathizers (and plenty of bystanders) across the continent. In the ‘90s, Italy’s Pantera student movement paralyzed campuses and city centers over a bill to corporatize the universities; in the 1980s, French students did much the same . Those generations were closer to the violence of a real war, but they were arguably in no way as desperate as today’s youth.

That desperation had some of the analysts I spoke to on edge. There has been a different quality to these protests than past movements for change: a toxic mix of despair and nihilism. Many of those arrested for vandalism have no prior criminal record or connections to political movements. It’s unclear what, if anything, unites them, besides a complete lack of faith in conventional authorities and their processes. “We don’t trust the institutions of this government,” the October 17 Movement communique reads , and “we don’t trust the traditional political structures [which] have been trying to profit from and monopolize struggles for decades.”

This is the fruit of the short-termism natural to gerontocracy. And it is a boon to opportunists of all kinds — the criminal, the bigot, the fascist. Generational conflict is far more universal, and more inevitable, than a race war, and it has already become a recruiting tool for haters and nihilists of every description. Whether these protests, historic though they may be, result in any meaningful change is doubtful; Stockemer, for his part, is neither impressed nor optimistic. “There’s this big outbreak of rage,” he said. “Then we wait two years, and there’s another outbreak of rage.”

But with each chime of the futile clock, Europe’s youth becomes more disillusioned, and more radicalized. Eventually, that clock will run out — and then, no pension will be generous enough to spare the elderly their discomfort.
